My grandmother, Nana Elsie, she was a bit of a character. Everyone in our town knew her for her garden – not because it was particularly *beautiful*, mind you, but because of the sculptures. She didn’t do flowers much, preferred…found objects. Old tires, bits of plumbing, rusty farm tools. And she’d weld them together, paint them these incredibly bright colors, and stick them amongst the tomato plants. 

But the strangest thing she ever made wasn't in the garden. It was a portrait. Of our cat, Mr. Fluffernutter.

Now, Mr. Fluffernutter was a perfectly ordinary tabby. A bit grumpy, liked naps, hated the vacuum cleaner. But Nana Elsie, she insisted he had “an aura.” And she decided he needed a portrait to capture it.

Only, she didn't use paint. Or charcoal. She used…butterflies.

I was maybe ten, and I remember being absolutely horrified when I walked into the garage. It smelled strongly of glue and something vaguely sweet, like overripe fruit. Nana Elsie had spent months collecting butterflies – not by catching them, thankfully, but finding ones that had already passed, mostly around the local nature preserve. She’d meticulously pinned them to a large piece of plywood, arranging their wings to create the likeness of Mr. Fluffernutter. 

It wasn’t a *good* likeness, not exactly. More…impressionistic. But the colors! The iridescent blues and greens, the velvety blacks, all arranged to suggest his stripes and his perpetually annoyed expression. It was unsettlingly beautiful. 

The whole thing was coated in layers of clear resin, so it didn't smell *too* bad after a while. It hung in her dining room for years. People would come over, expecting a quaint watercolor, and then…stare. Mr. Fluffernutter, forever preserved in a shimmering, fragile mosaic of wings. 

After Nana Elsie passed, my aunt tried to donate it to a museum. They politely declined. Said something about preservation concerns and…well, it was a bit macabre. Now it’s in my attic. I sometimes go up there just to look at it. It still gives me the creeps, but I can't deny it's a masterpiece, in its own peculiar way.

My grandfather, Silas, wasn’t a collector in the traditional sense. He didn’t go for coins or baseball cards. Silas collected…postage. Not the stamps themselves, mind you, but the *paper* the stamps had been affixed to. He called them “ghosts of correspondence.”

He started, he said, after inheriting a box of letters from a distant aunt. Most were mundane – bills, grocery lists, invitations to church socials. But the backs of the envelopes, with the faded glue and the partial stamp impressions, fascinated him. He believed each one held a tiny echo of the person who’d sent it, the person who’d received it, the moment in time it represented. 

Silas worked as a night watchman at the old county courthouse. He’d spend his breaks carefully peeling off stamps from discarded mail – things people sent to the various departments and then just tossed. He wasn’t damaging anything important, he always insisted. Just rescuing the ghosts.

He had thousands of these fragments, organized not by country or denomination, but by…feeling. He’d hold them up to the light, squinting, and say things like, “This one feels like regret,” or “This one smells faintly of lavender and ambition.” It was odd, to say the least.

The strangest thing happened in 1977, during the blizzard. The courthouse was completely shut down for a week. Silas was snowed in, of course, and spent the entire time meticulously arranging his collection on the floor of the records room. He was trying to create a “timeline of feeling,” he explained later. 

When the snow finally cleared and the courthouse reopened, the county clerk discovered something unbelievable. The arrangement of Silas’s “ghosts” perfectly predicted the outcome of every major local election for the next ten years. Not just the winners, but the vote totals, down to the last digit.

People dismissed it as coincidence, naturally. But Silas just smiled and said the paper remembered. He never explained how. He just kept collecting, quietly rescuing those little echoes of lives lived. After he passed, the collection was dispersed. I have a few pieces, but I can't say I've ever felt what he felt when he held them.
